title: Idle tales (Luke 23:55–24:12)
hookLine: the women tell the apostles, and the words seem like idle tales

lines: THEY WATCH WHERE HE IS LAID.
SPICES AT DAWN, AN EMPTY TOMB.
cards: Friday evening. The women from Galilee follow the body to the tomb and watch exactly where it's laid. They go home and prepare spices and ointments, and on the Sabbath, Luke says, they rest, according to the commandment.
Saturday is long and silent. Very early on Sunday, in the half dark, they walk back carrying the spices, to do the last thing love can do for the dead. The stone is rolled back.
The body is gone. And two men in shining clothes are standing there. Today, the first people to hear the news, and the first not to be believed.

teach.h: WHY SEEK THE LIVING WITH THE DEAD?
teach.b: The two men ask the question that turns the whole Gospel: "Why seek you the living with the dead? He is not here, but is risen." Remember what he told you in Galilee. And they remembered his words.
So the women go back and tell the eleven and all the rest. Luke names them: Mary Magdalen, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and other women with them.
Here's how the news lands: "And these words seemed to them as idle tales; and they did not believe them."
The Greek word is leros, and it's blunt: nonsense, silly talk, a word a medical writer of the time might use for the babbling of someone in a fever.
The apostles, chosen and trained for three years, hear the first announcement of the resurrection and call it nonsense. Luke doesn't hide it. He could have.
Peter does get up and run to the tomb. He stoops down, sees the linen cloths lying by themselves, and goes home wondering. Not believing yet.
Wondering. The women had no body and no proof: an empty space, two strangers, and a memory. Earlier in Luke, when Jesus told the twelve what would happen in Jerusalem, they understood none of it.
Now the women carry those same words back to them. The first people sent to say he is risen are the ones who came at dawn to anoint a corpse.

how: Catholics hear Luke's account of the empty tomb at the Easter Vigil in the year of Luke, the night the Alleluia returns after Lent.

games.why: the words seemed to them as idle tales, and they did not believe them. only Peter gets up and runs, and even he goes home wondering.

practice: Think of someone who told you something good lately and got a shrug back: a kid's story about their day, a friend saying things are finally getting better, a coworker excited about an idea you assumed wouldn't work.
Picture their face, hear it again, and this time let it be true and be glad with them. If you pray, thank God for their news.

wordCard.voice: Idle tales. What the apostles called the women's report of the empty tomb. In Greek, leros: nonsense. They were wrong. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: nonsense, silly talk, Luke's word for how the women's report sounded (Luke 24:11).

carryVoice: Your line: not idle tales. The first news of the empty tomb came from the women. See you tomorrow.
